title: Rosalind and the Postcards
premise: Rosalind Marchetti returns to her family's crumbling lake house after her grandmother's death, sorting a shoebox of unsent postcards addressed to a woman named Vesper. There she finds Bram, the young piano tuner her grandmother hired for years, who has been quietly learning a dying language from the old woman—recordings hidden in the piano's felt. As Rosalind reads the postcards aloud, she uncovers the family secret everyone arranged their lives around: Vesper was her grandmother's first love, erased when the house and its inheritance passed to the respectable branch of the family. When developers threaten the house and the language's last speaker is dying, Rosalind and Bram must decide whether to sell the inheritance or spend it preserving what it was built to silence. The novel ends with Rosalind mailing the postcards at last, converting the house into a small archive and school, and asking Bram the question her grandmother never got to ask.
about_author: Juniper Voss is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing ephemera in estate sales across the Great Lakes region. They write about the objects families leave behind and the silences they curate.

chapters.title: The Estate of Small Things
chapters.summary: Rosalind arrives at the lake house to inventory her grandmother Edith's belongings, resentful of a woman she barely knew. In a locked piano bench she finds forty unsent postcards, all addressed to a Vesper. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: dutiful grief cracking open into curiosity.

chapters.title: A Man Who Hears Radiators
chapters.summary: Bram arrives to service the piano one last time, as he has every season for three years. He recognizes the postcards' handwriting and says nothing, but lingers too long. POV: Bram. Emotional beat: the discipline of silence tested by a stranger with Edith's eyes.

chapters.title: Postcard One: The Pier, 1958
chapters.summary: Rosalind reads the earliest postcards aloud to the empty kitchen and begins reconstructing a summer: two young women, a borrowed boat, a language spoken only between them. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: the thrill of trespass into a hidden life.

chapters.title: The Felt and the Wire
chapters.summary: Tuning the piano, Bram discovers Edith's recordings hidden in the soundboard—her voice practicing a dying language with her teacher, Vesper. He realizes Edith was his secret teacher's own last student. POV: Bram. Emotional beat: vertigo at realizing he inherited an inheritance he never asked for.

chapters.title: The Cousins Arrive
chapters.summary: The Marchetti heirs descend for the reading of the will: Rosalind's uncle Gerald, poised to sell the house to developers, and her cousin Bea, desperate for her cut. The postcards go missing from the bench. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: the family's machinery of denial grinding into motion.

chapters.title: What the House Was Built Around
chapters.summary: Rosalind confronts Gerald, who admits the family knew about Vesper and paid her off decades ago; the house itself was the settlement. He warns Rosalind that digging will cost her the inheritance too. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: the corruption of power revealed as ordinary, administrative, familial.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Bram brings Rosalind to meet Maren, the elderly woman from whom he's been learning the language—Vesper's student, now the final fluent speaker, dying in a care home. Maren asks for one final student before her voice goes. POV: Bram. Emotional beat: terror and tenderness; a language balanced on two throats.

chapters.title: Postcards, Returned to Sender
chapters.summary: Rosalind finds the postcards in Gerald's briefcase; Bea, guilt-ridden, helps her steal them back. Reading the final unsent card—Edith asking Vesper to run away, dated the week of the payoff—Rosalind understands the question the whole family arranged itself around. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: fury transmuting into resolve.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: At the estate sale, Gerald announces the developer's offer. Rosalind stands and reads the last postcard aloud to the assembled family, then plays Edith's recordings on the untuned piano—Maren's language filling the house. POV: Bram, watching Rosalind. Emotional beat: the climax; invisibility abandoned, the question finally asked.

chapters.title: What We Send Forward
chapters.summary: The house becomes a small archive and language school; Gerald, shamed, quietly funds it. Rosalind mails all forty postcards to Vesper's surviving niece and begins her first lesson with Maren. On the pier, she asks Bram to stay. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: belonging chosen rather than inherited; the language, and the love, carried on.
